item.title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
item.description:
Skim new method — Rapids decodes distance-19 surface-code syndrome rounds in under 1 microsecond on a single FPGA with 20 microseconds latency, achieving a 240 times lower logical error rate than real-time union-find decoders.

Grade 0.552 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Chenyang Jin, Susanne F. Yelin, Andi Gu

Figure

Logical error rate versus throughput (c), error suppression factor Λ (d), and latency across code distances (e) for surface-code memory experiments at p=0.15% under SI1000 noise, comparing Rapids against prior real-time decoders.

Asks

Can a classical decoder keep pace with sub-microsecond syndrome cycles of superconducting quantum processors without sacrificing decoding accuracy or suffering high decision latency?

Before

Neural decoders could not exceed distance-11 at 1 microsecond throughput, or had latencies reaching 1 ms (AlphaQubit 2 RT); dedicated real-time hardware decoders sacrificed accuracy and reached at most distance-7 (or distance-11 with high error rates).

But

Evaluated primarily in simulation under SI1000 circuit-level noise; chip-to-chip latency floor modeled based on RTL simulation with Aurora links.

Tools

streaming convolutional neural network with GRU · FPGA co-design (AMD Versal VP1802) · quantization-aware training (4-bit/8-bit integer) · Monarch matrix layers · depthwise separable convolutions

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

item.title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control
item.description:
Skim new method — QuFrame closes the QEC feedback loop within a 1 µs round budget with fallback decoding in 144 ns, cutting the logical error rate by an average of 38.5% compared to a serialized blocking baseline.

Grade 0.540 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum error correction with silicon spin qubits”

Figure

Logical error rate versus physical error rate scaling factor for a rotated surface code (d=3, 9 rounds). QuFrame avoids stalling and tracks closest to the ideal zero-latency baseline, outperforming the serialized blocking controller across all noise levels.

Asks

How can a quantum controller track the Pauli frame in real time with bounded per-instruction latency under multi-core dispatch and decoders of variable latency?

Before

A serialized blocking controller, as modeled in XQsim (Byun et al., 2022), increased logical error rates by up to 4.1× over an ideal zero-latency controller.

But

Evaluated on a distance-3 rotated surface code with 17 physical qubits; IBM Heron coherence times prolonged 10× in simulations; fallback lookup table memory scales poorly for higher code distances without truncation.

Tools

QuFrameISA · Instruction Resolution Engine (IRE) · Pauli Frame Management Unit (versioned compare-and-swap) · AMD Alveo V80 FPGA · Helios simulator with IBM Heron noise model

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires continuous quantum error correction (QEC) to suppress physical noise. While Clifford-only workloads can defer corrections to software post-processing, universal computation breaks this paradigm: executing non-Clifford gates via magic-state gadgets introduces hard, real-time control-flow dependencies on error-corrected measurements. Consequently, the controller must extract syndromes, decode them, and update the Pauli frame in real time, closing the entire QEC loop within a strict 1 μs cycle. However, prior proposals on Pauli frame tracking remain largely theoretical, leaving the microarchitectural bottlenecks of tracking, resolving, and synchronizing frame updates across distributed control pipelines unaddressed. To this end, we present QuFrame, a control microarchitecture for real-time Pauli frame tracking that closes the QEC loop within 1 μs while sustaining QPU-rate throughput. By introducing QuFrameISA, we cleanly decouple instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management. Execution is distributed across per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines (IREs) that resolve instructions against the frame via a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit enables independent, lock-free concurrent commits. To strictly guarantee the 1 μs deadline, QuFrame pairs an asynchronous primary decoder with an on-chip fallback decoder that resolves in 144 ns, natively reconciling divergent updates in hardware without degrading logical error rates.

item.title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control
item.description:
Skim theory — Universal fault-tolerant quantum computation requires only a constant number (le20) of external control wires on an n-qubit chip, executing n/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀(n/ϵ) logical qubits with depth-3 periodic geometrically local operations.

Grade 0.552 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation”

Figure

Unrolling of a 1D brickwork quantum circuit into a 2D tile where qubits propagate continuously upward across a physical planar lattice.

Asks

How much external control is strictly necessary to operate a fault-tolerant universal quantum processor?

But

Asymptotic analysis. Assumes a noiseless global clock and physical noise on all operations below a universal positive constant. Logical gate time is n/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀(n/ϵ) without instantaneous classical wires.

Tools

spacetime unrolling into 2D tiles · concatenated quantum codes · periodic depth-3 cellular automata · fault-tolerant instruction decoding

Abstract

Contemporary classical information processors integrate tens of billions of transistors printed on a chip, yet are fully controlled through comparatively few external wires. This is possible because data flows through hard-coded operations in step with a global clock and is steered by external instructions. Today's solid-state quantum processors are different -- every qubit receives instructions from outside the chip via its own dedicated control line, and error correction adds a further torrent of syndrome data that is transported off-chip. Here we show that the external control of a quantum chip can be greatly simplified. We propose a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by modern classical processors, in which quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device, propelled by local gates in a planar array. Our quantum processor receives an input stream of classical instructions via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit. Except for those few qubits coupled to external wires, all qubits evolve under a periodically-applied geometrically-local depth-3 circuit, which is fixed at the time the device is fabricated. Assuming a noiseless global clock (so that every operation is applied on schedule, though imperfectly), we establish an accuracy threshold theorem: For physical noise below a universal threshold -- afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire -- a chip with n physical qubits can run any quantum algorithm that uses~n/sfpolylog(n/ε) logical qubits, where ε is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time~n/sfpolylog(n/ε); an alternative design, in which quantum operations remain strictly local and noisy, but on-chip wires broadcast noiseless classical signals instantaneously, reduces the time per logical gate to sfpolylog(n/ε).

item.title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models
item.description:
Skim new method — Non-binary detector error models reduce Tanner graph edges by 4.3 to 5.3× and 4-cycles by 9 to 13×, lowering logical error rates under belief propagation while accelerating BP with OSD by up to 9.4× on a CPU.

Grade 0.505 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Stefano Tinelli, Francisco Lázaro, Francisco García Herrero

Figure

Logical error rate (LER) versus physical error rate p comparing binary (dashed) and non-binary (solid) DEMs under flooded belief propagation with and without OSD post-processing across surface, color, and bivariate bicycle codes.

Asks

Can syndrome extraction circuit noise be decoded more effectively by representing each fault location with a single non-binary random variable over its native alphabet rather than decomposing it into independent binary mechanisms?

Before

Standard binary detector error models generated by Stim decompose non-binary Pauli channels into independent Bernoulli mechanisms, creating numerous 4-cycles inside fault locations.

But

Circuit-level Pauli noise on Clifford circuits; verified on d=5 rotated surface code, d=5 6.6.6 color code, and [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code; parallel flooded scheduling with max 100 iterations.

Tools

split-merge-regroup transformation · scalar-message non-binary belief propagation · ordered statistics decoding (OSD-CS) · Stim circuit simulation

Code. https://github.com/s-tinelli/nbdem

Abstract

A key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) is that the syndrome extraction circuits are themselves faulty. Such circuit-level noise is commonly described by a detector error model (DEM). In Stim and in almost all related works, DEMs are binary: every non-binary circuit error (e.g., CNOT gate), is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. In this work, we introduce non-binary DEMs, in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is modeled by one random variable over its original alphabet, e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT gate. We also propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging the error components that flip the same detectors and observables. Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts. When the channels factorize, we prove that binary and non-binary DEMs are equivalent under degenerate quantum maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding, but not under quantum MAP decoding. Although the variables are non-binary, belief propagation (BP) still exchanges a single scalar message per edge. Our numerical results with surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes show that non-binary DEMs have two main advantages. First, their Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, which is advantageous for hardware implementations. Second, their performance under BP, with and without OSD post-processing, is better than that of their binary counterparts, and BP with OSD runs up to 9.4× faster in a CPU.

item.title: Accelerating Quantum Error Correction Simulations under Coherent Noise with Compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product States
item.description:
Skim new method — Compiled CAMPS accelerates trajectory sampling by over an order of magnitude compared to uncompiled CAMPS and physical MPS at equal bond dimension χ, while accurately estimating surface-code logical failure rates up to d=9 and bivariate bicycle [[72,12,6]] codes under coherent noise at modest bond dimensions.

Grade 0.490 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum error correction with silicon spin qubits”

Figure

Logical error rate pL (left) and median sampling time per shot (right) as functions of bond dimension χ for a d=r=5 surface code. Compiled CAMPS matches the untruncated state-vector reference at low bond dimension and is over an order of magnitude faster per shot than uncompiled CAMPS.

Asks

How can one mitigate entanglement growth and large qubit counts to achieve scalable trajectory sampling of quantum error correction circuits under coherent noise using tensor networks?

Before

Uncompiled CAMPS updated Clifford disentanglers dynamically per shot without free-qubit recycling, requiring larger bond dimensions χ and suffering from order-of-magnitude slower sampling per trajectory.

But

Demonstrated for rotated surface codes up to distance d=9 with coherent ZZ rotations and a [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code with coherent Y rotations under phenomenological depolarizing/coherent noise models, using PyMatching and BP-OSD decoders.

Tools

Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product States (CAMPS) · cross-shot Clifford compilation · qubit recycling via mid-circuit measurement release · rotation fusion and operator-span minimization · block-MPS tensor updates

Abstract

Reliable assessment of quantum error correction requires understanding how coherent errors affect logical performance. Although tensor networks naturally capture coherent interference, entanglement growth and large qubit counts make repeated sampling costly. Here we develop a compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product State (CAMPS) framework that reuses Clifford transformations across shots, recycles qubits released by measurements, evolves a compressed residual state, and accelerates sampling through rotation fusion and compilation tailored to the MPS layout. Surface-code benchmarks under fixed-sign coherent noise yield accurate logical error estimates at small bond dimensions, while random-sign simulations up to distance d=9 and on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code match the Pauli-twirling approximation results. Compared with uncompiled CAMPS, compiled CAMPS converges at smaller bond dimensions and achieves order-of-magnitude sampling speedups at equal bond dimension, opening a scalable route to studying coherent error propagation in larger fault-tolerant circuits.

arxave:action.title: Assess CAMPS for spin-qubit coherent-noise models

item.arxave:action: Adapt the compiled CAMPS workflow to spin-qubit-relevant coherent error models such as residual ZZ coupling and crosstalk, then compare logical error estimates against Pauli-twirling approximations for a surface-code patch sized to the target device.
item.arxave:abstract: Reliable assessment of quantum error correction requires understanding how coherent errors affect logical performance. Although tensor networks naturally capture coherent interference, entanglement growth and large qubit counts make repeated sampling costly. Here we develop a compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product State (CAMPS) framework that reuses Clifford transformations across shots, recycles qubits released by measurements, evolves a compressed residual state, and accelerates sampling through rotation fusion and compilation tailored to the MPS layout. Surface-code benchmarks under fixed-sign coherent noise yield accurate logical error estimates at small bond dimensions, while random-sign simulations up to distance d=9 and on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code match the Pauli-twirling approximation results. Compared with uncompiled CAMPS, compiled CAMPS converges at smaller bond dimensions and achieves order-of-magnitude sampling speedups at equal bond dimension, opening a scalable route to studying coherent error propagation in larger fault-tolerant circuits.
